data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories in action is defensible without smuggling induction by reframing 'preference' as a methodological rule to maximize the severity of future tests, not as an inductive inference of truth or reliability; the cost of this defense is the admission that Popperian science offers no rational guarantee for practical success (e.g., bridge safety), only a commitment to the fastest possible error elimination.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent acts on the theory expecting it to succeed (e.g., the bridge will hold) rather than expecting it to potentially fail safely, they have smuggled in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the formal definition of verisimilitude remains incoherent (per Tich\u00fd/Miller), the comparison of 'better' corroborated theories lacks logical footing.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'preferring for criticism' and 'preferring for action' cannot be maintained in high-stakes scenarios where failure is catastrophic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'context of discovery/action' (where agents must act) and 'context of justification' (where logic applies). It argues that choosing the best-corroborated theory is a non-inductive strategic rule: since the goal is truth via falsification, one must test the theory that has survived the hardest attempts, as it contains the most potential falsifiers. Acting on it is not betting on its truth (induction) but betting on its capacity to reveal error quickly if false. This resolves the tension by denying that 'acting on' implies 'believing probable'.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
